chunks: "I'd give four reasons. First, the gate is insulated, so it's voltage-controlled. Once the gate capacitance is charged, it takes basically zero current to hold the MOSFET on.
A microcontroller pin can drive one directly, whereas a power BJT carrying 10 amps might need half an amp of base current the whole time.
Second, when it's fully on it behaves like a resistor, not a fixed voltage drop. Modern parts have milliohms of R DS(on) , so 10 amps through 5 milliohms is 0.
5 watts, versus several watts for a saturated BJT. And because R DS(on) goes up with temperature, you can parallel MOSFETs and they share current. Third, they switch fast.
Conduction is by majority carriers, so there's no stored minority charge to pull out like in a saturated BJT. That's what makes hundreds-of-kHz to MHz converters practical.
Fourth, and the biggest by volume, is digital. NMOS and PMOS pair up into CMOS, where one transistor is always off, so a gate draws almost no static current.
And MOSFETs scale: shrink them and they get smaller, faster and cheaper, which is why a chip can have billions.
They're not perfect: at very high voltage IGBTs or SiC win on conduction loss, and BJTs still have an edge in some low-noise analog work.
But for most switching and all digital, MOSFETs are the default."
